• Ulpian: about one-third of the Digest.
• Only Ulpian is quoted more extensively than Paul.

cards.q: What share of the Digest consists of passages from Ulpian?
cards.a: About one-third.

cards.q: Where did Ulpian come from, and what was his writing like?
cards.a:
A Syrian, probably born in Tyre – an example of provincials rising in the Empire.
• His writings were huge in volume.
• Perhaps lacking Paul's critical insight, but models of clarity, simplicity and reliability.
• Unusually for a jurist, he was interested in philosophy: law as the highest form of philosophy, concerned with right and wrong.

cards.q: When did Ulpian mainly write, and what does Honoré suggest about his aim?
cards.a:
Mainly AD 213–17.
• Possibly meant as a single-handed codification of the law.
• Honoré (controversial): after the CONSTITUTIO ANTONINIANA of AD 212 (which Ulpian may have drafted) there was a need for a full exposition of the law for the Empire's peoples.

cards.q: What were Ulpian's chief works?
cards.a: AD EDICTUM and AD SABINUM.

cards.q: What offices did Ulpian hold, and how did he die?
cards.a:
• Probably head of the office of petitions in the early 3rd century.
• Later praetorian prefect under Alexander Severus.
• Murdered by his own guards, probably in AD 223, allegedly in front of the emperor.

cards.q: Who formed the 'formidable late classical trio' of jurists?
cards.a: Papinian, Paul and Ulpian.

cards.q: Who was Modestinus?
cards.a:
Perhaps the last distinguished jurist of the classical period.
• Not in the class of Papinian, Paul and Ulpian.
• Ulpian calls him his 'pupil' (D.47.2.52.20).
• He held only minor office but reportedly had influence at the imperial court.
• He wrote student handbooks, practice manuals and monographs, not large commentaries.

cards.q: What did Ulpian answer his pupil Modestinus in D.47.2.52.20 (the male ass among the mares)?
cards.a:
No theft without theftuous intent.
• Someone who drove off another's male ass and set it loose among his own mares to breed is not guilty of theft unless he had the intent to steal.
• Ulpian applied the same to horses: liability for theft only with guilty intent.

13.title: The post-classical era: why the jurists vanished; Law of Citations; legislation
13.text: The three centuries between the end of the classical period and Justinian's codification are usually seen as a time of decline. There was a great deal of legislation, for example on the Church after Rome's conversion. The emperor's law became the only source, the jurists lost importance and the classical intellectual spirit largely disappeared. The decline was worse in the West, where the Empire was politically fragile and eventually broke up. In the East, flourishing law schools partly halted it. Why were there no outstanding jurists? Borkowski weighs four explanations: classical legal science had exhausted itself, political instability, talent drawn into the Church after the conversion, and Diocletian's bureaucracy, which required anonymous drafters as the Principate turned into the Dominate. None explains everything. Even under Diocletian, Hermogenianus made a name with the CODEX HERMOGENIANUS. Post-classical literature was anonymous and unoriginal (COLLATIO, FRAGMENTA VATICANA). Because summaries distorted the classical texts, rules on authority became necessary. Constantine banned the notes of Paul and Ulpian on Papinian. The Law of Citations (AD 426) gave primary authority to five jurists: Gaius, Papinian, Paul, Ulpian and Modestinus. The majority decided; on a tie, Papinian's view decided; otherwise the judge was free. Critics see this 'counting of heads' as a sign of intellectual fatigue. Legislation grew, especially in the East, and became verbose and conflicting. There were attempts to settle the status of rescripts, and in AD 439 decrees were made inapplicable in another emperor's territory without his consent.

terms.def: Three centuries between the end of the classical period and Justinian's codification; period of decline, emperor's legislation the sole source.
Phases of the Empire; the transition to the Dominate (Diocletian) meant juristic activity lost its individuality.
Collection of imperial decrees by Hermogenianus (under Diocletian), c. AD 295.

terms.term: COLLATIO LEGUM MOSAICARUM ET ROMANARUM / FRAGMENTA VATICANA
terms.def: Anonymous post-classical works (probably early 4th c.) summarizing classical works and imperial legislation.
Gave primary authority to Gaius, Papinian, Paul, Ulpian and Modestinus; majority rule, Papinian decisive in a tie.

cards.q: How is the post-classical era generally characterized?
cards.a:
As a period of decline.
• It spans the three centuries between the end of the classical period and Justinian's codification.
• Much legislation driven by huge changes, e.g. laws defining the powers of the Church after the conversion.
• The emperor's legislation was the only source of law, and the jurists lost importance.
• The intellectual spirit of the classical period was largely missing.

cards.q: Why was the post-classical decline worse in the West than in the East?
cards.a:
West: the Empire was increasingly fragile politically and eventually fell apart.
East: the decline was partly halted by flourishing law schools, which prepared the ground for Justinian's work.

cards.q: Which explanations does Borkowski discuss for the lack of outstanding jurists after the classical period?
cards.a:
• Classical legal science could not go on for ever – after Paul and Ulpian, what was left to do?
• Political instability from the 3rd century – but the late Republic was unstable and full of jurists.
• The conversion to Christianity drew talent into the Church – but this does not explain the gap between Modestinus' death (AD 244) and the conversion.
• Diocletian's bureaucratic reforms required anonymous drafters (Principate → Dominate) – but this does not explain the generation before Diocletian.

cards.q: When did Modestinus die?
Which explanation of the jurists' disappearance does Borkowski consider most satisfactory, and what is its weakness?
cards.a:
Diocletian's bureaucratic reforms.
• They required anonymous drafters: everything had to appear to come from the emperor, so juristic work lost its individuality in the move from Principate to Dominate.
• Weakness: it does not explain why there were no outstanding jurists in the generation before Diocletian.

cards.q: Who was Hermogenianus?
cards.a:
A talented jurist under Diocletian.
• Author of the CODEX HERMOGENIANUS, a collection of imperial decrees, some of which he may have drafted himself.
• Honoré: secretary of the office of petitions; his rescripts were 'a legal education in themselves'.
• He is quoted in Justinian's Digest.

cards.q: Name two works of post-classical juristic literature and their character.
cards.a:
COLLATIO LEGUM MOSAICARUM ET ROMANARUM and FRAGMENTA VATICANA.
• Probably early 4th century.
• Anonymous and unoriginal: summaries of classical works and imperial legislation, with a risk of distorting the originals.

cards.q: Why did Gaius' Institutes gain authority in the post-classical period?
cards.a:
Post-classical summaries had caused confusion.
• Gaius' Institutes hardly needed summarizing, so it was seen as a model exposition of classical law.

cards.q: What did Constantine prohibit with regard to juristic writings?
cards.a: The use of the notes of Paul and Ulpian on Papinian.

cards.q: When was the Law of Citations enacted, and which five jurists did it name?
cards.a:
AD 426.
• Gaius, Papinian, Paul, Ulpian, Modestinus.

cards.q: How did the Law of Citations resolve conflicts between juristic opinions?
cards.a:
• Only the five named jurists had primary authority; their quotations of other jurists also counted.
• If they conflicted, the majority view prevailed.
• With no majority, the judge decided as he pleased – unless Papinian had expressed a view, which then had to be followed.

cards.q: Why has the Law of Citations been criticized?
cards.a:
It counted heads instead of weighing the merits of opinions.
• It was mechanical, though practical.
• Critics see it as a symptom of the age's alleged intellectual fatigue.

cards.q: What happened to imperial legislation in the post-classical period?
cards.a:
It grew, especially in the East.
• The forms stayed broadly the same, with a greater variety of RESCRIPTA.
• Decrees became verbose, full of rhetoric glorifying the emperor.
• Many carelessly drafted decrees caused confusion and conflicts.

cards.q: How did post-classical emperors try to limit the authority of rescripts?
cards.a:
• Constantine: rescripts 'contrary to the law' were invalid – ambiguous, since rescripts were themselves law and later law normally repealed earlier law (C.Th.1.2.2).
• End of the 4th century: rescripts authoritative only for the case for which they were issued (C.Th.1.2.11).
• Theodosius II: rescripts generally authoritative if stated to be of general application (cf. C.1.14.12pr).

cards.q: What did Theodosius II decide in AD 439 about decrees in a divided Empire?
cards.a:
Decrees were not to apply in another emperor's territory without his consent.
• Earlier practice: decrees were issued in the name of all the emperors and were valid throughout the Empire.

14.title: Codes of imperial law, Christianity, Eastern influence, barbarian codes, vulgarization
14.text: Several collections of imperial decrees were made in the post-classical era. The CODEX GREGORIANUS (c. AD 291) gathered all surviving decrees of the previous hundred years. The CODEX HERMOGENIANUS (c. AD 295) contained the decrees of the years just before it. Both were 'unofficial', not issued in any emperor's name, though they must have had imperial approval. The most important was the THEODOSIAN CODE (AD 438), which collected all imperial legislation since Constantine in 16 books, divided into titles with the decrees in chronological order. It is the most important code in Roman legal history apart from the Twelve Tables and Justinian's codification, and was a model for Justinian. Theodosius II also planned a compilation of juristic writings but never carried it out. 2.4.3: Four factors shaped later law: Christianity, Eastern customs, the barbarian invasions and the law schools. Christianity produced ecclesiastical law and punished divorce without cause, but did not abolish divorce or slavery. Eastern influence gave the law a Byzantine colour, especially the law of persons (marriage gifts, dowry). In D.1.3.32.1 'Julian' says custom has almost statutory force. The attribution is suspect: the text is probably the Digest compilers' work, reflecting the revival of custom. The barbarian kingdoms issued codes for their Roman subjects: the lex Romana Visigothorum (506, Alaric II), the lex Romana Burgundiorum and the Edictum Theodorici. 'Vulgarization' is an ambiguous label for these influences. In the East, the law schools of Beirut and Constantinople led a 5th-century revival of legal learning.

terms.def: c. AD 291; contained all extant imperial decrees of the previous hundred years; 'unofficial'.
AD 438; all imperial legislation in force enacted since Constantine; 16 books divided into titles, decrees chronological within titles.
AD 506, promulgated by the Visigoth chief Alaric II; legislation (mainly from the Theodosian Code) plus abridged extracts from Gaius and Paul.
Early 6th c.; for Roman citizens in what is now eastern France; systematic titles based mainly on classical sources.
Probably by the Ostrogoth chief Theodoric; applied to 'barbarians' as well as Romans; aid to interpretation of existing law.
Term for the influence of Christianity, Eastern custom and barbarian codes on post-classical Roman law; ambiguous (debasement / departure from classical norms / regional divergence / crude practice).

cards.q: Distinguish the CODEX GREGORIANUS from the CODEX HERMOGENIANUS.
cards.a:
CODEX GREGORIANUS (c. AD 291): all surviving imperial decrees of the previous hundred years.
CODEX HERMOGENIANUS (c. AD 295): decrees from the years just before its publication.
• Both were 'unofficial' – not issued in the name of a particular emperor (possibly Diocletian) – but must have had imperial approval.

cards.q: What did the Theodosian Code contain, and when was it issued?
cards.a:
AD 438.
• All imperial legislation then in force that had been enacted since Constantine.

cards.q: How was the Theodosian Code structured?
cards.a:
16 books, each divided into titles.
• Within each title the decrees were listed in chronological order.
• The scheme was not new: it had been used in Diocletian's compilations, which followed some classical works.

cards.q: Why is the Theodosian Code important?
cards.a:
After the Twelve Tables and Justinian's codification, it is the most important code in Roman legal history.
• A model, to some extent, for Justinian's codification.
• A prime historical source for the period's tensions, e.g. taxation and Church matters.

cards.q: What did Theodosius II plan besides his code of imperial legislation?
cards.a:
A compilation of juristic literature.
• It was never carried out.
• Justinian, who knew of it, wanted to outdo him.

cards.q: Which four factors particularly influenced post-classical Roman law?
cards.a:
• The conversion to Christianity.
• Eastern customs.
• The 'barbarian' invasions.
• The work of the law schools.

cards.q: How did Christianity affect Roman law?
cards.a:
• A complex ecclesiastical law on the relationship between Church and State.
• Rules on the status of clergy and church functionaries; new offences protecting church property and personnel.
• Changes to the law of persons, e.g. strict sanctions for divorce without cause.
• But divorce and slavery were not abolished; slaves' legal position improved under Justinian.

cards.q: Give examples of Eastern (Greek) influence on late Roman law.
cards.a:
• Constantine and his successors favoured Eastern customs, giving Roman law a Byzantine colour.
• The bridegroom's substantial gift to the bride on marriage was recognized by late imperial legislation.
• The dowry (given to the husband by the wife or her family) was affected by Greek custom: legislation reduced the husband's rights in it.

cards.q: What does D.1.3.32.1 (attributed to Julian) say about custom?
cards.a:
Long-established custom has almost the force of a statute.
• Reason: statutes bind only because the people accepted them, so what the people approved without writing should bind everyone too.

cards.q: Why is the attribution of D.1.3.32.1 to Julian suspect, and who probably wrote it?
cards.a:
It does not fit what we know of Julian.
• Given the centralizing tendencies of his time, he is unlikely to have given custom 'almost statutory force'.
• The authors were most probably Justinian's Digest compilers – an example of an interpolation.
• It reflects the revived importance of custom after its near disappearance as a source following the Twelve Tables.

cards.q: What was the LEX ROMANA VISIGOTHORUM?
cards.a:
A code for Roman citizens promulgated in AD 506 by the Visigoth chief Alaric II.
• A mix of legislation (mainly from the Theodosian Code) and abridged extracts from classical jurists, especially Gaius and Paul.
• A debased form of Roman law, but of lasting influence: used in parts of the former Western Empire into the early medieval period.

cards.q: Distinguish the three 'barbarian' codes mentioned by Borkowski.
cards.a:
LEX ROMANA VISIGOTHORUM (AD 506, Alaric II): for Roman citizens; legislation plus extracts from Gaius and Paul.
LEX ROMANA BURGUNDIORUM (early 6th century): for Roman citizens in what is now eastern France; arranged systematically in titles, mainly from classical sources.
EDICTUM THEODORICI (same period, probably the Ostrogoth Theodoric): applied to 'barbarians' as well as Romans; meant to aid interpretation of existing law.

cards.q: What senses can the term 'vulgarization' carry?
cards.a:
• Most derogatory: the debasement of Roman law, especially in the 'barbarian' codes.
• Technical: open departure from classical norms.
• The divergence between law in remote parts of the Empire and law around Rome and Constantinople.
• The supposedly crude, unscientific practice of Roman law in the later Empire.

cards.q: Which law schools led the 5th-century revival of legal learning in the East?
cards.a:
Beirut and Constantinople.
• The revival came especially under Theodosius II.
• Other schools (Rome, Alexandria, Athens) existed, but these two were by far the most eminent.

15.title: Justinian's codification: Tribonian, Codex vetus, Fifty Decisions, the Digest
15.text: The eastern law schools taught by lecturing on the classical texts in detail. This return to the originals renewed legal science and made Justinian's work possible. 2.5: The codification was Justinian's most durable achievement and made possible the Reception of Roman law in medieval Europe and beyond. He began it in AD 528, a few months after becoming emperor; he had in effect ruled during his predecessor's reign and probably planned it in advance. The law was in confusion: the Theodosian Code did not restate the whole law, the Law of Citations had sped up the decline of legal science, and there was a mass of new legislation. Tribonian led most of the project. He was a consul and quaestor and knew the classical jurists well; Justinian overlooked his alleged corruption, his supposed pagan sympathies and his unpopularity, according to Procopius. The stages were the Codex vetus, the Fifty Decisions, the Digest, the Institutes, the New Code and the Novellae. The first two were only preparatory and are not part of the CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS. The Codex vetus was set up by the CONSTITUTIO HAEC: ten men under John of Cappadocia, including Tribonian and Theophilus, gathered the imperial enactments still in force. It was published in AD 529, repealed all earlier codes, and survives only in one index page. The Fifty Decisions (AD 530) resolved disputed points of juristic law; no copy survives. Honoré credits the idea of the Digest to both Justinian and Tribonian. The Digest (or PANDECTS) is by far the most important source of Roman law: an anthology of mainly late classical jurists, preserved in the 'Florentine' manuscript. As a model for the Empire it failed, being too large, too complex and too badly arranged.

terms.def: Justinian's chief minister for much of the codification; consul and quaestor; learned in classical juristic works; chaired the Digest commission.
Name sometimes given to Justinian's codification (Digest, Institutes, New Code, Novellae); the Codex vetus and Fifty Decisions are not part of it.
Imperial pronouncement creating the ten-man commission for the first Code (Codex vetus).
First Code of Justinian, AD 529: all imperial enactments still in force; repealed all previous imperial legislation; not extant except an index page.
Series of decrees of AD 530 abolishing obsolete rules and resolving controversies in juristic literature; no copy survives.
Centrepiece of Justinian's work: an anthology of juristic literature, mainly late classical, updated for contemporary use; by far the most important source of Roman law.
Manuscript made not long after the Digest's compilation, through which the Digest survived intact.

cards.q: How did the eastern law schools prepare the ground for Justinian?
cards.a:
They taught through lectures that examined the classical texts in detail.
• This return to the original texts renewed the science of law and created the intellectual climate for Justinian's works.

cards.q: Why is Justinian's codification historically so important?
cards.a:
It was by far the most durable achievement of his reign.
• It made possible the Reception of Roman law in medieval Europe and later in many other parts of the world.

cards.q: When did Justinian begin the codification?
cards.a:
AD 528, a few months after he came to the throne.
• He had effectively ruled during much of his predecessor's short reign and probably planned it beforehand.

cards.q: Why did Justinian consider a codification necessary?
cards.a:
The law was in confusion.
• The Theodosian Code was not a full restatement of the law.
• Legal science had declined, a decline sped up by the Law of Citations.
• There was a mass of new imperial legislation.
• So it was hard to find out the law on any given matter.

cards.q: Who was Tribonian?
cards.a:
Justinian's chief minister for much of the codification.
• Held several important offices, including consul and quaestor.
• A very learned man, familiar with the classical jurists.
• Justinian overlooked his alleged corruption, supposed pagan leanings and unpopularity with the Constantinople nobility (according to the Greek writer Procopius).

cards.q: List the main stages of Justinian's codification in order.
cards.a: Codex vetus → Fifty Decisions → Digest → Institutes → New Code → Novellae.

cards.q: Which stages of Justinian's codification are not part of the CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS?
cards.a:
The Codex vetus and the Fifty Decisions.
• They were only preparatory.

cards.q: What does Justinian say in the CONSTITUTIO DEO AUCTORE (c. 1) about the first stage of the codification?
cards.a:
The imperial laws had become hopelessly confused.
• The law since the foundation of Rome was of enormous length and beyond human understanding.
• So the first task was to free the constitutions of the earlier emperors from faults and collect them in one CODEX, without repetition or harmful disagreement.

cards.q: How was the CODEX VETUS made?
cards.a:
• The CONSTITUTIO HAEC created a commission of ten men to collect all imperial enactments still in force.
• An updating exercise: a revision especially of the Theodosian Code and the codes of Diocletian's reign.
• Led by John of Cappadocia; members included Tribonian and Theophilus (professor at Constantinople).
• It had wide powers to remove obsolete and confusing material.

cards.q: When was the CODEX VETUS published, and what was its effect?
cards.a:
AD 529, after a little over a year's work.
• It superseded all earlier imperial legislation – the Theodosian Code and all others were repealed.

cards.q: How do we know the content of the CODEX VETUS?
cards.a: Only from one surviving index page – no copy of the code survives.

cards.q: Why is the first Code called 'vetus' ('old')?
cards.a: The label was added later to distinguish it from the New Code of AD 534.

cards.q: What were the Fifty Decisions?
cards.a:
Decrees of AD 530 that abolished obsolete rules and resolved disputed points in juristic literature.
• Published, probably the same year, as a separate collection.
• No copy survives.

cards.q: Who conceived the idea of the Digest?
cards.a:
Probably both Justinian and Tribonian (Honoré).
• The Codex vetus and the Fifty Decisions may have been Justinian's original plan; Tribonian, a scholar with an outstanding library, may have persuaded him to summarize the jurists' literature.
• Or it reflects Justinian's own ambition to outdo Theodosius II, who planned but never made a compilation of classical juristic literature.

cards.q: What is the Digest (PANDECTS)?
cards.a:
The centrepiece of Justinian's work: a legal encyclopaedia.
• An anthology of juristic literature, mainly of the late classical period, updated for contemporary use by the compilers.
• By far the most important source of Roman law.
• It culminated the rebirth of legal learning in the eastern law schools of the 5th century.

cards.q: How has the text of the Digest survived?
cards.a: Intact in a manuscript made not long after its compilation – the 'Florentine' text.

cards.q: Did the Digest achieve Justinian's aim?
cards.a:
No – he meant it as a model for his empire, but it was too large, too complex and too badly arranged.
• Still, its huge mass of material proved invaluable to later ages.

16.title: Compiling the Digest: commission, task, sources; interpolations
16.text: Two constitutions are the main evidence for how the Digest was compiled: DEO AUCTORE (December AD 530) and TANTA (December 533). Tribonian chose 17 commissioners, himself included: academics, practitioners and ministers. Four were professors: Dorotheus and Anatolius from Beirut, and Theophilus and Cratinus from Constantinople. Their task (Deo auctore 4) was to read the works of the old jurists whom the emperors had authorized to interpret the law, extract their substance, remove repetition and contradiction, and produce one work in place of them all. They did not fully succeed: despite Tanta 15 the Digest contains repetitions and conflicting passages. Tribonian supplied rare books himself (Tanta 17). The claim that about 2,000 books were excerpted is an exaggeration; 1,500–1,600 is more likely. The index lists 38 jurists. Because every quoted jurist now had equal authority, the Law of Citations was repealed, but Ulpian, Paul and Gaius still supply over half the excerpts. The arrangement follows the scheme of the classical commentaries; the project was launched by the constitution AD SENATUM of 22 July 530. 2.5.3.2: Under Tanta 10 the commission could amend texts. These changes, called interpolations, were not marked, so a jurist may be quoted saying something he never wrote. They are detected by comparison with other texts, by breaks in logic, and by language or terminology that is not classical. Not all were made by Justinian's commission; some came from earlier eastern academics. After an early 20th-century obsession, scholars now take a cautious view. Supplement (not in Borkowski): a Digest citation such as D.1.2.2.4 gives book.title.fragment.paragraph, and 'pr' (principium) is the opening part before § 1.

terms.def: Imperial decree of December AD 530 authorizing the compilation of the Digest; describes the commission and its task.
Decree of December AD 533 on the completed Digest (claims of no contradictions, 2,000 books, power to amend).
The imperial decree which set the Digest project in motion (Pugsley).
Amendments made to juristic texts when they were excerpted, without acknowledgment; the compilers had power to amplify or curtail texts (Tanta 10).
Issued with the Digest; shows excerpts from 38 different jurists.
D. book . title . fragment . paragraph, e.g. D.1.2.2.4; 'pr' = principium (opening part before § 1), e.g. D.1.4.1pr.

cards.q: Which two constitutions tell us most about the compilation of the Digest, and when were they enacted?
cards.a:
CONSTITUTIO DEO AUCTORE (December AD 530) and CONSTITUTIO TANTA (December AD 533).
• They tell us at least what Justinian chose to reveal.

cards.q: What did the CONSTITUTIO DEO AUCTORE (c. 3) order Tribonian to do?
cards.a:
Choose suitable colleagues.
• From the most eloquent professors and the ablest advocates of the highest court.
• They worked in the palace on the whole task, under Tribonian's close supervision.

cards.q: How many commissioners compiled the Digest, and who were they?
cards.a:
17, including Tribonian.
• A mix of leading academics, practitioners and government ministers.

cards.q: Name the four law professors on the Digest commission and their schools.
cards.a:
• Beirut: Dorotheus and Anatolius.
• Constantinople: Theophilus and Cratinus.

cards.q: What task does the CONSTITUTIO DEO AUCTORE (c. 4) give the Digest commission?
cards.a:
To make one work out of the old jurists' books.
• Read and work through the books on Roman law by the old jurists whom the emperors had authorized to compose and interpret laws.
• Extract their whole substance.
• Remove repetition and discrepancy as far as possible.
• Compile one single work to replace them all.

cards.q: Did the compilers succeed in removing all repetition and contradiction from the Digest?
cards.a:
No.
• The Digest has many repetitions and inconsistencies.
• Tanta 15 nevertheless claims that no contradiction found a place in it.
• Centuries of careful study have not reconciled some conflicting passages.

cards.q: What does the CONSTITUTIO TANTA (c. 17) say about Tribonian's part in collecting sources?
cards.a:
Tribonian supplied a very large number of books.
• Many were unknown even to the most learned men.
• All were read and the most valuable parts excerpted.

cards.q: How many books were reportedly read and excerpted for the Digest, and what is the realistic figure?
cards.a:
Claimed: about 2,000 books.
• This is exaggerated; the evidence suggests 1,500–1,600.

cards.q: From how many jurists were excerpts taken for the Digest?
cards.a:
38 different jurists, according to the index of authors and works issued with the Digest.
• Many more are quoted indirectly through those writers.

cards.q: Why did the Digest require the repeal of the Law of Citations?
cards.a: All jurists quoted in the Digest had to have equal authority.

cards.q: Which jurists dominate the Digest?
cards.a:
The jurists named in the Law of Citations, especially Ulpian, Paul and Gaius.
• These three together account for more than half of the excerpts.

cards.q: What scheme did the overall arrangement of the Digest follow?
cards.a: The traditional scheme found in the major classical commentaries.

cards.q: Which imperial decree set the Digest project in motion, according to Pugsley?
cards.a: The constitution AD SENATUM of 22 July 530.

cards.q: What power did the Digest compilers have over the texts (CONSTITUTIO TANTA 10)?
cards.a:
Power to amend them.
• If anything seemed superfluous, imperfect or unsuitable, they could expand or shorten it and put it in its most correct form.
• Purpose: to give practitioners a workable text, not just a summary of the literature.

cards.q: What are interpolations?
cards.a:
Changes made to juristic texts when they were excerpted for the Digest.
• The compilers named the jurist for each excerpt but did not mark the changes.
• So a jurist may be quoted saying something he did not write.

cards.q: How can interpolations be detected?
cards.a:
• Comparing Digest passages with surviving classical or Byzantine texts.
• A lack of coherence or logic in a passage (risky – classical jurists could lapse too).
• Style, construction and vocabulary compared with classical Latin and the style of the particular jurist.
• Legal terms not known until late law.

cards.q: Why is the linguistic test for interpolations both useful and dangerous?
cards.a:
Useful: the compilers' first language was probably Greek (Latin was the official language of the courts), and 6th-century Latin differed from Paul's and Ulpian's.
Dangerous: classical jurists may also have written sloppy, unidiomatic Latin.

cards.q: Were all interpolations made by Justinian's commission?
cards.a:
Not necessarily.
• Some may have been made earlier, perhaps by academics in the eastern law schools.
• The commission may have used texts that were already interpolated.

cards.q: How has scholarly attitude to interpolations changed?
cards.a:
From obsession to caution.
• Early 20th century: the hunt for interpolations became an obsession.
• Interpolations matter if one studies only classical law, for which the Digest is hardly a reliable guide.
• But classical law is not the whole of Roman law.
• Interpolations are now seen as necessary amendments for a working code, not as corruption.
• Interpolation criticism has given way to a more balanced and cautious approach.

cards.q: How do you read a Digest citation such as D.1.2.2.4 or D.1.4.1pr? (supplement – Borkowski uses but does not explain the system)
cards.a:
D. book . title . fragment . paragraph.
• D.1.2.2.4 = Digest, book 1, title 2, fragment 2, paragraph 4 (here: Pomponius' Manual on the Twelve Tables).
• 'pr' = principium, the opening part of a fragment before § 1: D.1.4.1pr = book 1, title 4, fragment 1, principium (Ulpian on the emperor's decisions).

17.title: Ban on commentaries, speed of compilation, Nika riots, Bluhme's masses
17.text: Scholars now assume that the classical core of most texts survived and that most changes were cosmetic. 2.5.3.3: Justinian wanted the Digest to be a model, so in Deo auctore 12 he banned commentaries on it, because past commentators' conflicting opinions had thrown the law into confusion. He did allow translations and explanatory notes on difficult passages. Under Tanta 21, doubtful points were to be referred by judges to the emperor, who alone could both make and interpret law. Even so, commentaries appeared before his reign ended. 2.5.3.4: The Digest took three years instead of the ten planned, although most commissioners were not working on it full-time. Several explanations have been offered. The Peters theory says an earlier digest (a 'Pre-Digest') had been made at a law school, but there is no evidence for it. Another view is that the commissioners did not actually read the books; yet Tanta 17 says many books were new to them. Honoré argues that three years was feasible given the commission's organization and books averaging only about 10,000 words. The Nika riots of AD 532 may also have pushed Justinian to finish quickly. The rival Blues and Greens joined against him over heavier taxes on the rich, and one complaint was that Tribonian neglected the administration of justice for the Digest. Honoré thinks the riots had little effect, a view Borkowski finds hard to accept. 2.5.3.5: Bluhme, an early 19th-century German scholar, showed that each title draws on three 'masses' of works, each probably handled by a subcommittee: Sabinian, Edictal and Papinian, followed by a smaller Appendix mass.

terms.def: Speculation that an earlier digest had been compiled at a law school before Justinian, explaining the speed of compilation; no hard evidence.
Rebellion in Constantinople in which the rival Blues and Greens united against Justinian; nearly ended his reign; possibly a catalyst for speedy completion of the Digest.
Three groups of works (Sabinian, Edictal, Papinian) plus a smaller Appendix mass, from which the excerpts within each Digest title were drawn, each probably by a subcommittee.
Commentaries on the ius civile (Paul, Ulpian and others) arranged according to Sabinus' system.
Works on the ius honorarium, specifically the praetorian edict.
Problematic literature – the genre in which Papinian excelled.

cards.q: What is the current scholarly view of how far the compilers altered the classical texts?
cards.a:
The classical 'core' of most texts probably remained intact.
• Most changes were purely cosmetic.
• Reason given: the scope of the commission's mandate and the speed of the compilation.

cards.q: What did Justinian decree about commentaries on the Digest (Deo auctore 12)?
cards.a:
He banned them.
• No lawyer was to confuse the brevity of the work with his own wordy commentary.
• In earlier times the conflicting opinions of commentators had thrown the whole law into confusion.

cards.q: What did Justinian allow despite the ban on commentaries?
cards.a: Translations and explanatory notes on difficult passages.

cards.q: How were doubtful points in the Digest to be resolved (Tanta 21)?
cards.a:
Judges were to refer them to the emperor.
• Only imperial authority could both make laws and interpret them.
• The rules against confusion probably covered the other parts of the codification too.

cards.q: Did Justinian's ban on commentaries work?
cards.a: No – commentaries began to appear even before the end of his reign.

cards.q: How long did the Digest take to compile, compared with the original plan?
cards.a:
Three years instead of the planned ten.
• This was remarkably short, as most commissioners probably did not work on it full-time.

cards.q: What is the Peters theory, and why is it doubted?
cards.a:
It holds that an earlier digest ('Pre-Digest') had been compiled at a law school before Justinian, perhaps by professors later on the commission.
• Attractive, but there are no hard facts and no copies.
• Suppression would have needed a long conspiracy, and Tribonian was 'hardly a burner of books'.

cards.q: What are the main explanations for the speed of the Digest's compilation?
cards.a:
• Peters theory: an earlier 'Pre-Digest' already existed – no evidence.
• The books were not actually read, since the commissioners knew them already – but Justinian says many books were unknown to them.
• Honoré: three years was feasible given the high level of organization and books averaging only about 10,000 words.
• The Nika riots (AD 532) pushed Justinian to finish quickly.

cards.q: According to Honoré, how long were the books read by the Digest compilers on average?
cards.a: About 10,000 words.

cards.q: What were the Nika riots, and how might they have affected the Digest?
cards.a:
A rebellion in AD 532 that nearly ended Justinian's reign.
• The rival factions (Blues and Greens, who cheered chariot teams in the Hippodrome) united against the emperor, mainly over a stricter tax regime on the wealthy.
• They may have pushed Justinian to finish the Digest fast, as a prestige success (Pugsley); the sloppy final editing supports this.
• Against: Justinian had urged speed before the riots; Honoré thinks their impact was slight.

cards.q: How was Tribonian connected with the causes of the Nika riots?
cards.a: One alleged cause was poor administration of justice, because Tribonian was devoting his time to the Digest.

cards.q: What did Bluhme discover about the Digest?
cards.a:
That the material within each title is not haphazard.
• It falls into three groups ('masses') of works, each probably compiled by a subcommittee of Tribonian's commission.
• Bluhme was a German scholar of the early 19th century.

cards.q: Name and describe Bluhme's three masses.
cards.a:
• Sabinian: commentaries on the IUS CIVILE by Paul, Ulpian and others, arranged on Sabinus' system.
• Edictal: works on the IUS HONORARIUM, specifically the praetorian edict.
• Papinian: problematic literature, the genre in which Papinian excelled.

cards.q: In what order do the masses usually appear within a Digest title?
cards.a:
Sabinian → Edictal → Papinian → Appendix (last).
• The Appendix mass is a smaller group of miscellaneous works that did not fit the three main masses.

18.title: Organizing the commission; the Institutes; the New Code and Novellae
18.text: Bluhme thought the Appendix works reached the commission late and were excerpted by the Papinian committee, which had the lightest load. The outline of his theory is widely accepted and helps explain the speed of the work, but the Appendix part has been criticized. The 11 practitioners were probably added to subcommittees as needed, while the other six commissioners worked in three pairs, one pair per subcommittee. Tribonian was in overall charge and Justinian supervised actively. Honoré sees a carefully planned operation, like a modern law commission. In his reconstruction, the Sabinian and Edictal committees each got through seven books a week and the Papinian committee five. Excerpting took about 18 months, the first draft about eight more, and the Digest was enacted in December 533. Osler and Pugsley challenge his numbers and his picture of the planning; Pugsley argues the Papinian committee was set up only later. 2.5.4: Justinian reorganized legal education into three years of formal teaching followed by two of private study, with the Digest at the core. Dorotheus and Theophilus wrote the Institutes as an introductory textbook, under Tribonian's supervision. Like Gaius' Institutes, on which they were mainly based (together with his RES COTTIDIANAE), they have four books, but they are also divided into titles. They were promulgated the same day as the 50-book Digest and had force of law. 2.5.5: The New Code (AD 534, 12 books, titles, chronological order) replaced all earlier codes. Justinian's later reforms were issued as NOVELLAE CONSTITUTIONES. His codification was meant to make the law manageable and accessible (Tanta 13), but even practitioners struggled with the Digest.

terms.def: Introductory textbook by Dorotheus and Theophilus under Tribonian; four books divided into titles; based especially on Gaius; promulgated the same day as the Digest with force of law.
Revision of the Codex vetus by Tribonian and a small commission; twelve books, titles, constitutions in chronological order; superseded all previous codes.
'The new decrees' – Justinian's individual decrees after the New Code (e.g. reforms of family law and inheritance); best regarded as part of the codification.
The Digest or Pandects consisted of fifty books (Prooemium to the Institutes).

cards.q: How were the 17 Digest commissioners probably organized?
cards.a:
• The 11 practitioners were probably co-opted onto the subcommittees when needed.
• The other six formed three pairs, each assigned to one subcommittee.
• Tribonian had overall responsibility; Justinian actively supervised.

cards.q: Why has the Appendix part of Bluhme's theory been criticized?
cards.a:
Bluhme said the Appendix works reached the commission late and were excerpted by the Papinian committee, which had the lightest workload.
• Critics: it is unlikely the commission discovered books late that it had not known about before.
• The rest of Bluhme's theory is widely accepted and helps explain the speed of the work.

cards.q: How does Honoré reconstruct the Digest commission's workload and timetable?
cards.a:
• Committees worked in parallel on their book lists.
• Sabinian and Edictal committees: seven books per week each; Papinian committee: five.
• Each committee had two senior commissioners (chairman and junior member), helped by barristers.
• Excerpting about 18 months → first draft about 8 months → final editing → enactment December 533.

cards.q: How long did the excerpting and the first draft of the Digest take, according to Honoré?
cards.a:
Excerpting about 18 months; first draft about 8 months.
• Then final editing, before enactment in December 533.

cards.q: How does Honoré judge Tribonian's chairmanship of the Digest commission?
cards.a:
'One of the most brilliant feats of organisation in the history of civil administration.'
• He likens the commission to a modern law commission.

cards.q: How do Osler and Pugsley criticize Honoré's account of the Digest commission?
cards.a:
Osler: the numbers behind Honoré's theory have no foundation; he doubts that each subcommittee split the work equally between its two seniors.
Pugsley: doubts the degree of planning; argues the Papinian committee did not exist at the start and was set up only after a trial run showed a third committee was needed.

cards.q: How did Justinian reorganize legal education?
cards.a:
Three years of formal tuition, then two years of private study.
• The Digest was to be the core of the new programme.

cards.q: Who wrote Justinian's Institutes, and why?
cards.a:
Dorotheus and Theophilus, under Tribonian's supervision.
• The Digest was too daunting for beginners, so an introductory textbook was needed.

cards.q: How many books does the Digest have?
cards.a: Fifty books (the Digest or Pandects).

cards.q: On what sources were Justinian's Institutes based (Prooemium §§ 4–6)?
cards.a:
On all the classical books of Institutes, especially Gaius.
• Gaius' Institutes and his 'Daily Matters' (RES COTTIDIANAE), plus many other commentaries.

cards.q: Compare the structure of Justinian's Institutes with Gaius' Institutes.
cards.a:
Same: four books.
Different: Justinian's Institutes are also divided into titles; Gaius' are not.

cards.q: What was unusual about the legal status of Justinian's Institutes?
cards.a:
Though a student textbook, they had the force of law.
• They were promulgated on the same day as the Digest.

cards.q: Why was a New Code needed, and who made it?
cards.a:
A flurry of legislation followed the Codex vetus, so a revision was soon needed.
• Tribonian did it with a small commission.

cards.q: When was the New Code promulgated, and how was it structured?
cards.a:
AD 534.
• Twelve books, subdivided into titles on specific topics.
• Imperial pronouncements in chronological order within each title.
• It superseded all previous codes, included constitutions issued after the first Code, and removed repetitions and obsolete matter.

cards.q: What were the NOVELLAE CONSTITUTIONES?
cards.a:
'The new decrees' – Justinian's individual decrees after the New Code.
• His reign lasted more than thirty years after the New Code, and he kept legislating, e.g. important reforms of family law and inheritance.
• They are best treated as part of the codification, though not everyone agrees.

cards.q: What did Justinian intend his codification (CORPUS IURIS CIVILIS) to achieve (Tanta 13)?
cards.a:
To make the law manageable and accessible.
• One system of law made known to all, relieving them of confusion.
• Laws that are straightforward, brief and easily available.
• Books cheap enough for rich and poor alike.

cards.q: How did the codification work out in practice?
cards.a:
Parts of it were too complex.
• Even practitioners struggled with the Digest, and by Justinian's death it was scarcely used in the courts.
• But his reforms of substantive law and legal education were far-reaching; as a law reformer he is supreme among Roman emperors, possibly apart from Augustus.

It points to the online resources for the 6th edition (timeline, biographies of key figures, glossary of Latin terms, Latin originals of the Digest and Institutes extracts, examples of textual analysis) and lists further reading: Watson on the Twelve Tables, Millar on the emperor, Syme on fictions about jurists' lives, Harries/Wood, Honoré and Matthews on the Theodosian Code, and Honoré (2010) on the character and compilation of Justinian's Digest. The right page begins chapter 3, 'Roman Litigation', which goes beyond the topic of the extract. Horace's 'good man' serves as a witness, a guarantor and a judge, but Romans avoided appearing as litigants; Cicero advised avoiding litigation like the plague. The advocacy profession emerged in the mid-Republic, trained in Greek rhetoric and given to ritual abuse (VITUPERATIO) of the opponent.

terms.def: Ritual abuse of the opponent (looks, habits, breeding) by Roman advocates in court.

cards.q: Which book does Borkowski recommend for further reading on Justinian's Digest project?
cards.a: Honoré, T. (2010), Justinian's Digest: Character and Compilation (Oxford University Press).

cards.q: How did Romans view acting as a litigant, according to Borkowski (ch. 3)?
cards.a:
With reluctance.
• Being a witness, guarantor or judge was a civic duty (Horace's 'good man').
• Litigation was seen as undignified; Cicero advised avoiding it like the plague, even with the law on one's side.
• Fear for one's reputation discouraged lawsuits.

cards.q: What was VITUPERATIO?
cards.a:
Ritual abuse of the opponent by Roman advocates – mocking his looks, habits, breeding and so on.
• Example: in Pro Quinctio Cicero likened his client's opponent to a clown.
• Because it was ritual, it was probably less intimidating than it sounds.
